analysis.one_liner: Bans shipping Great Lakes water out of the country by tanker until states agree on a conservation plan.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; it was referred to a House subcommittee in November 1999 and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001, with no vote ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned the export of Great Lakes water in bulk — tanker loads shipped overseas without processing — from the United States. It treated the lakes as a public resource held in trust by the eight Great Lakes states and the Canadian provinces, and it set the ban to expire at the end of 2001 unless Congress approved an agreement among the states to manage withdrawals under a common conservation standard. The bill was referred to the House International Relations Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the Great Lakes region, whose drinking water, economy, and ecosystem depend on lake levels staying stable; the eight Great Lakes states and Canadian provinces, whose authority over the water would be reinforced; and anyone downstream who would otherwise bear the cost of water being shipped away in bulk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Great Lakes region residents and state governments

how_it_helps.text: Declares the Great Lakes 'precious public resources, held in trust' by the Great Lakes states and the Canadian provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and bars export of bulk fresh water from the Basin from the United States.

Responds to growing worldwide demand for fresh water, which the bill's findings say poses 'a unique challenge to the management of the Great Lakes,' and notes that the ecological effects of bulk exports are unknown and that there is no credible binational way to regulate them.

Keeps day-to-day control of withdrawals and diversions with the Great Lakes state governors (whose authority dates to the Water Resources Development Act of 1986) and the Canadian premiers, rather than opening the lakes to export markets.
Ties the federal ban to a durable fix: the moratorium lifts when Congress approves an interstate agreement creating a common conservation standard for Great Lakes withdrawals.

analysis.who_pays: Any company or entrepreneur hoping to sell Great Lakes water abroad in bulk — tanker shippers and large-volume water exporters — who would be shut out of the market entirely while the moratorium lasts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bulk water exporters and tanker shippers

drawbacks.text: The ban is a stopgap, not a permanent law: it expires automatically on December 31, 2001 unless Congress approves a state conservation compact, so it only buys time for the states to act.

It defers the real decision to the eight governors and Canadian premiers, whom the bill expressly says must keep control of day-to-day management, so the federal ban is only as strong as the state agreement that follows.
The definition of 'bulk fresh water' covers only water shipped by tanker or similar mass transport without further processing, so water that is processed before shipping would not fall under the ban.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, time-limited protection with a clear fallback: it blocks bulk export while the Great Lakes states negotiate a lasting conservation standard, and it lifts if Congress approves that standard. The cost falls almost entirely on a prospective export industry, not on ordinary consumers, and the main weakness is that it depends on the states finishing the job before the sunset date. A well-designed temporary measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House International Relations Committee, then to its trade subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2001 — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI) introduced the bill on September 29, 1999, joined by original cosponsors Reps. Ehlers, Hoekstra, Knollenberg, Smith of Michigan, and Upton.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on International Relations.
On November 16, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on International Economic Policy and Trade, where no further action was taken.
The bill attracted 13 cosponsors (11 Republicans and 2 Democrats) but never advanced out of committee, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 without the bill receiving any vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prospective bulk water exporters kept the regulatory door open, and the lakes remained under state-by-state management without the federal backstop the bill would have provided — the Great Lakes states also lost the leverage of a federal moratorium while negotiating a conservation compact.

for.name: Rep. Dave Camp
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor twice (October 1999 and March 2000).

for.name: 13 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including the five original cosponsors named on the introduced bill.

against.name: House Committee on International Relations
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; no hearing or markup is recorded.

against.name: Subcommittee on International Economic Policy and Trade
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from November 16, 1999 until the end of the Congress without action.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the 13 cosponsors split 11 Republicans and 2 Democrats, and the sponsor and all named original cosponsors were Michigan Republicans, so support was regional rather than a clean party split.

industries.industry: Bulk water exporters and tanker shippers
industries.note: The bill bans exporting Great Lakes water in bulk by tanker or similar mass transport, shutting this prospective industry out of the market entirely. Its gain would come at the direct expense of a public resource relied on by millions of people.

industries.industry: Great Lakes state water managers and governors
industries.note: The bill reaffirms that authority over the lakes rests with the eight Great Lakes governors under the Water Resources Development Act of 1986 and the Canadian premiers, and it lifts the federal ban only when Congress approves a state conservation compact. It entrenches state-level control as the permanent mechanism for deciding who can take Great Lakes water.
